source.title: THE LYAPIN’S NOTEBOOK: A COLLECTION OF UNSOLVED PROBLEMS IN SEMIGROUP THEORY

accepted.question_text: Describe which types of equations or systems of equations over a finite semigroup admit an algorithm that, for arbitrary values of the constants, decides whether the system is solvable in some finite extension of the original semigroup.

evidence.quote:
Problem 1.1. (S. Kublanovsky, M. Sapir) Describe the types of equations or systems of equations
for which there exists an algorithm that decides for any values of the constants whether the given
system is solvable in some finite extension of the original semigroup.

             Potential properties of semigroups include embedding problems into various recursive
classes of finite semigroups. A homomorphic image of a subsemigroup T of a semigroup S is called
a divisor of S (or factor of S).

accepted.question_text: Describe the divisors of the following subclasses of finite 0-simple semigroups: (1) finite Brandt semigroups; and (2) finite 0-simple semigroups given in Rees matrix form by a matrix whose entries are only 0 and 1.

evidence.quote:
Problem 1.2. (S. Kublanovsky) Describe the divisors of the following subclasses of finite 0-simple
semigroups:

    (1) the class of finite Brandt semigroups;
    (2) the class of finite 0-simple semigroups presented in the Rees representation by a matrix
         that consists only of zeros and ones.

Divisors of the class of all finite 0-simple semigroups are described by positive universal formulas
(see [5]).

accepted.question_text: Determine whether there is an algorithm that decides, for a given finite semigroup, whether it embeds into a power semigroup over some finite group, or more generally over some periodic group.

evidence.quote:
Problem 1.3. (S. Bershadsky, S. Kublanovsky) Is there an algorithm that decides whether a given
finite semigroup is embeddable into a power semigroup over some finite group (periodic group) (see
Chapter 5 of this notebook)?
             Not every finite semigroup has this property, but every semigroup is a divisor of the power
semigroup over a periodic group (see [1]). For divisors of power semigroups over finite groups the
answer is positive (see [3]).

           We say that a variety satisfies a property locally if any finitely generated semigroup in
the variety satisfies this property. The following problem naturally arises.

accepted.question_text: Describe, for known predicates, the semigroup varieties that are locally residually finite, meaning that every finitely generated semigroup in the variety is residually finite with respect to the predicate under consideration.

evidence.quote:
Problem 2.2. (S. Kublanovsky) Describe locally residually finite varieties of semigroups for known
predicates.
In the global case, such description is obtained in [11], [12]. For the equality predicate in the local
case, the description is obtained in [32]. Locally residually finite varieties of rings were described
in [13].

           Let RSn denote the variety generated by all 0-simple semigroups satisfying the identity
x2 = xn+2 . Such varieties and their subvarieties are called Rees-Sushkevich varieties (see [14]).

accepted.question_text: Let RS_n be the variety generated by all 0-simple semigroups satisfying x^2 = x^(n+2). Describe the covers of RS_n both in the lattice of all semigroup varieties and in the lattice of varieties satisfying x^2 = x^(n+2).

evidence.quote:
Problem 2.3. (S. Kublanovsky) Describe the covers of the semigroup variety RSn in the lattice
of varieties of all semigroups and in the lattice of varieties satisfying the identity x2 = xn+2 .
It follows from the results of [15] that in the latter lattice the number of covers is finite. It is also
known that every subvariety of RS1 has only finitely many covers (see [14]).

Problem 2.4. (S. Kublanovsky) Describe periodic varieties generated by regular semigroups.

           A word u is called blocking (respectively, non-blocking or avoidable) if, for every finite
alphabet the set of words over this alphabet that do not contain images of u under substitutions,
is finite (respectively, infinite). These concepts play an important role in the theory of semigroup
varieties and in theoretical combinatorics (see [4], [34]).

accepted.question_text: Let c(u) be the number of distinct letters occurring in a non-blocking word u, and let m(u) be the smallest alphabet size for which there exists an infinite word avoiding all substitution images of u. Determine m(u) for a non-blocking word u containing c(u) letters.

evidence.quote:
Problem 2.5. (I. Melnichuk) Let c(u) denote the number of distinct letters occuring in the word
u. Let m(u) denote the minimal number of letters in a finite alphabet A for which there exists an
infinite word over A that does not contain images of u under substitutions. Determine the number
m(u) for a non-blocking word u containing c(u) letters.
Some estimates were obtained in works [[29], [30], [27], [3]].

          In the following series of problems we consider varieties of ordered semigroups, that is,
semigroups equipped with a partial order compatible with the semigroup operation. Such varieties
are defined by identities together with identical inequalities. Identical inequalities are often called
identical relations of precedence. For example, the semigroup of real numbers on the segment
S = [0, 1] with multiplication satisfies the identical inequality xy ≤ x.
          E.S. Lyapin proposed the problem of studying varieties defined by identities and identical
inequalities in the late 1970s.

accepted.question_text: Determine when a system of identical inequalities, also called identical relations of precedence, is equivalent to a system of identities for ordered semigroups.

evidence.quote:
Problem 2.7. (E.S. Lyapin) Under what conditions is a system of identical inequalities (identical
relations of precedence) equivalent to a system of identities?
This problem is solved for systems consisting of a single identical inequality in [17].

Problem 3.4. (S. Kublanovsky) Obtain estimates for the values of the endomorphic function for

          In 1969, M.M. Lesokhin (a student of E. S. Lyapin) posed the problem of describing
commutative semigroups that have no endomorphisms other than power functions, i.e. such endo-
morphisms that map each element to a fixed power of this element ([21], problem 1.34). Below we
call commutative semigroups whose endomorphisms are all power functions Lesokhin semigroups.
          The first nontrivial example of a Lesohin semigroup was constructed by B.K Boguta (a
student of Prof. Lesokhin) in the paper [1]. Lesokhin’s problem in the class of regular semigroups
was solved by A.I. Kuptsov (a student of Prof. Lesokhin) in [9].
          It can be verified by direct calculations that a finitely generated Lesokhin semigroup is
either finite with a single idempotent or has no idempotents. Finite Lesokhin semigroups and
2-generated Lesokhin semigroups without idempotents were described by A.A. Borisov in [2] and
[3]. The next series of problems was set by A.A. Borisov (a student of Lyapin).

accepted.question_text: Describe finitely generated Lesokhin semigroups without idempotents, where a Lesokhin semigroup is a commutative semigroup whose endomorphisms are all power maps sending each element to a fixed power of itself.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.5. (A.A. Borisov) Describe finitely generated Lesokhin semigroups without idempo-
tents.
It is proved in [5] that finitely generated separative Lesokhin semigroups without idempotents should
be isomorphic to subsemigroups of an infinite monogenic semigroup.

accepted.question_text: Describe commutative semigroups all of whose endomorphisms are injective.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.6. (A.A. Borisov) Describe commutative semigroups all of whose endomorphisms are
injective.
It is proved in [5] that finitely generated commutative semigroups all of whose endomorphisms are
injective are precisely subsemigroups of an infinite monogenic semigroups or finite ordinal sums of
such semigroups.

             A commutative semigroup is called an E-semigroup if it is isomorphic to the semigroup
of all its endomorphisms under pointwise multiplication. For Abelian groups, this concept was
introduced in [7]. In [5], A.A. Borisov described several classes of finitely generated commuta-
tive E-semigroups: finite ones; semigroups without idempotents; cancellative semigroups; and
Archimedean semigroups.

accepted.question_text: Describe finitely generated commutative separative E-semigroups, where an E-semigroup is a commutative semigroup isomorphic to the semigroup of all its endomorphisms under pointwise multiplication.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.7. (A.A. Borisov) Describe finitely generated commutative separative E-semigroups.
It is proved in [5] that for a finitely defined commutative semigroup the problem of deciding whether
the semigroup of all its endomorphisms (under pointwise multiplication) is Archimedean is algo-
rithmically solvable.

accepted.question_text: Describe commutative semigroups whose semigroup of endomorphisms under pointwise multiplication is a free semigroup.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.10. (A.A. Borisov) Describe commutative semigroups whose semigroups of endomor-
phisms (with pointwise multiplication) are free semigroups.

             It is proved in [5] that for a finitely generated commutative semigroup S the following
conditions are equivalent:

    (1) the semigroup of all endomorphisms of S under pointwise multiplication is a free commu-
        tative semigroup;
    (2) the semigroup of all endomorphisms of S under pointwise multiplication is an infinite
        monogenic semigroup generated by an identical endomorphism.

In other words S is a Lesokhin semigroup.
             Let S be a semigroup without idempotents. For elements a, b ∈ S we write a < b if
a = ab = ba. It is easy to verify that < is a strict partial order on S. Hence one can speak about
comparable and incomparable elements and about chains in S.

of length 1. If S contains a chain of length r (r ≥ 1) but no chain of length r + 1, we say that

accepted.question_text: Determine whether every finitely generated, or finitely presented, semigroup without idempotents has finite chain rank, where a < b means a = ab = ba and the chain rank is the maximum length of a finite chain under this strict partial order, or infinite if arbitrarily long chains exist.

Problem 3.11. (A.A. Borisov) Is it true that the chain rank of any finitely generated (or finitely
presented) semigroup without idempotents is finite?

accepted.question_text: Describe commutative semigroups that have exactly four endomorphisms.

Problem 3.12. (A.A. Borisov) Describe commutative semigroups that have exactly four endo-

It is proved in [4] that every finite commutative semigroup with more than four elements has at

          In his book Semigroups, E.S. Lyapin emphasized that establishing connections between
the properties of endomorphism semigroups and the properties of the underlying structured sets
is one of the most important directions in semigroup theory. This direction may be viewed as a
natural generalization of the ideas of Galois theory.

accepted.question_text: For natural classes of mathematical structures, such as ordered sets and relatively free algebras, and for subsemigroups of their endomorphism semigroups, determine: (1) which subclasses are defined up to isomorphism by these semigroups; and (2) which subsemigroups of endomorphism semigroups determine the structures up to isomorphism.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.13. (E.S. Lyapin) For natural classes of mathematical structures - such as ordered
sets, relatively free algebras, and for subsemigroups of endomorphism semigroups of these structures
- determine:

     (1) Subclasses of structures defined up to isomorphism by these semigroups;
     (2) Subsemigroups of endomorphism semigroups that determine these structures up to isomor-
         phism.

For various classes of partially ordered sets E.S. Lyapin found endomorphism semigroups that
determine these classes up to isomorphism (see [11], [12], [13]).

          For a mathematical structure A, denote by End(A) (respectively Aut(A)) the semigroup
(respectively group) of its endomorphisms (automorphisms) under composition. The sequence

                  End(A), End(End(A)), . . .   (respectively Aut(A), Aut(Aut(A)), . . .)

is called the tower of endomorphisms (respectively tower of automorphisms) of A.

accepted.question_text: Describe the endomorphism semigroup and the tower of endomorphisms or automorphisms: (1) for endomorphism semigroups of semigroups that are free in basic classes, especially idempotent, commutative Clifford, and Clifford semigroups; and (2) for endomorphism semigroups of algebras free in basic classes of mathematical structures.

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.14. (G. Mashevitzky) Describe the endomorphism semigroup and the tower of endo-
morphisms (automorphisms)

     (1) for endomorphism semigroups of semigroups free in basic classes of semigroups, in partic-
         ular in the classes of idempotent, commutative Clifford, and Clifford semigroups;
     (2) for endomorphism semigroups of algebras free in basic classes of mathematical structures.

For the class of all semigroups and inverse semigroups, the description of semigroups of endo-
morphisms were obtained in [14] and [15]. Towers of automorphisms of free inverse semigroups
are described in [19].

accepted.question_text: Describe: (1) transformation semigroups that are closed in the pointwise topology; and (2) endomorphism semigroups that are closed in a Zariski-type topology.
accepted.context_brief: Closure in pointwise and Zariski-type topologies

evidence.quote:
Problem 3.15. (G. Mashevitzky)

    (1) Describe transformation semigroups that are closed in the pointwise topology.
    (2) Describe endomorphism semigroups that are closed in a topology of Zarisky type.

Motivation and definitions can be found in [6], [16], [17], [18]. Transformation semigroups closed in
the pointwise topology are precisely the semigroups of endomorphisms of mathematical structures
(see [18]). It was shown in [16] that the Zariski-type topology is weaker than the pointwise topology
and conditions were obtained under which these topologies coincide. Several special cases of the
problem were solved in [18].

evidence.quote:
Problem 7.3. (E.S. Lyapin) Characterize pargoids of transformations that admit an internal
semigroup extension.
          Some sufficient conditions are given in [12].

          A class of algebraic systems is called a class of models if its signature contains only
relations. A partial binary operation can be represented by a ternary relation, which allows par-
goids, groups, and semigroups to be viewed as models. This approach provides new classification
possibilities, as demonstrated in the papers [2], [3] by O.M. Gornostaev (a student of Prof. A.E.
Evseev, himself a student of Lyapin).
          A model M with a ternary relation is said to be representable in a groupoid A (in
particular, in a semigroup or a group), if there exists an injective homomorphism from M into
the corresponding ternary model of A. This definition can be generalised to universal algebras of
arbitrary signature.
          If C is a variety, then the class of models representable in C is a quasivariety of models,
that is, the representability condition can be expressed by quasiidentities (see [3]).
          An involution is a unary operation x → x−1 that satisfies the identity (x−1 )−1 = x.
Semigroups equipped with an involution are called involuted semigroups. Clifford semigroups and
inverse semigroups are examples of involuted semigroups.

accepted.question_text: Describe the varieties of involuted semigroups for which the quasivarieties of models representable in those varieties are finitely axiomatizable.
